vulnerabilities.title: Auto-mint max limit is per-transaction, allowing unbounded total minting
vulnerabilities.description: autoMint enforces `autoMintMaxLimit >= amount` but does not track cumulative auto-minted supply. Because `nonce` simply increments each call and there is no aggregate cap or per-window accumulator, the autoOwner can call `autoMint` repeatedly up to the limit. This renders `autoMintMaxLimit` ineffective as a total issuance cap and allows arbitrary inflation of the token supply.
vulnerabilities.exploitScenario: The owner sets `autoMintMaxLimit` to 1,000,000 tokens to constrain the hot autoOwner wallet. The autoOwner (or a compromised autoOwner key) calls `autoMint(to, 1_000_000, nonce, chainId)` repeatedly. Each call mints another 1,000,000 tokens and increments `nonce`. After 100 iterations, 100,000,000 tokens have been minted, diluting all holders and breaking the stablecoin peg.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Introduce a cumulative auto-mint accumulator (e.g., per-day or total minted) and enforce `autoMintMaxLimit` against that total. If the limit is intended only as a per-transaction cap, rename the variable and error to avoid ambiguity and add explicit documentation.

vulnerabilities.title: autoBurn can destroy the contract owner's balance without allowance
vulnerabilities.description: autoBurn is callable only by the autoOwner role, yet it burns tokens from `owner()` rather than from the caller or a specified `from` account. There is no allowance check or signature from the owner. If the autoOwner is a distinct hot wallet or service, this grants it unilateral power to destroy owner-held funds.
vulnerabilities.exploitScenario: The owner (treasury) holds a large token balance. The autoOwner key is compromised or the autoOwner service is malicious. It calls `autoBurn(treasuryBalance, nonce, chainId)`, which passes `owner()` to `_burn` and permanently destroys all tokens held by the owner.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Change `autoBurn` to burn from `msg.sender`, or add a `from` parameter and require an allowance/signature from that account. Align the burn semantics with `autoMint`, where the autoOwner already chooses the destination.

vulnerabilities.title: V2 initializer can be called by anyone, force-enabling EIP-7598
vulnerabilities.description: StablecoinV2.initializeV2 uses `reinitializer(2)` but has no access-control modifier. After a proxy is upgraded to V2, any account can call `initializeV2()` once and set `eip7598EnableFlag = true`, enabling signature-based transfers before the owner intends to activate them.
vulnerabilities.exploitScenario: The owner upgrades the proxy to the StablecoinV2 implementation but plans to keep EIP-7598 disabled until off-chain integrations are audited. An attacker monitors the upgrade transaction and calls `initializeV2()` first, enabling EIP-7598. Any pre-signed authorizations that signers expected to be unusable while disabled can now be executed, potentially moving user funds unexpectedly.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add `onlyOwner` to `initializeV2`, or invoke it atomically as part of the upgrade transaction by the proxy admin.

vulnerabilities.title: V1 initializer can be front-run, granting attacker full ownership
vulnerabilities.description: Stablecoin.initialize is unprotected and sets `msg.sender` as both the `owner` and `autoOwner`. If the proxy is deployed without being initialized in the same transaction, a malicious actor can call `initialize` first and obtain all privileged roles.
vulnerabilities.exploitScenario: The team deploys the implementation and an upgradeable proxy pointing to it, but initialization is submitted separately. An attacker front-runs the initialize call with `initialize("Stablecoin","STB")`, becoming both `owner` and `autoOwner`. The attacker then mints arbitrary tokens, freezes legitimate addresses, and takes full control of the contract and its funds.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Initialize the proxy atomically in the deployment transaction, or use a factory/deployment script that ensures only the deployer can call `initialize`. Alternatively, protect `initialize` so that it can only be called by the intended deployer address.
